points: SMS Posen was one of four Nassau-class battleships.
The Nassau class comprised the first dreadnoughts built for the German Imperial Navy, also known as the Kaiserliche Marine.
Posen was laid down on 11 June 1907.
Posen was built at the Germaniawerft shipyard in Kiel.
Posen was launched on 12 December 1908.
Posen entered service with the High Seas Fleet on 31 May 1910.
Posen's main battery consisted of twelve 28 cm (11 in) guns.
The main guns were mounted in six twin turrets.
Posen's main turrets formed an unusual hexagonal arrangement.
Posen served with her three sister ships for most of World War I.
Posen saw extensive service in the North Sea during World War I.
Posen participated in several sorties with the fleet.
Posen's North Sea sorties culminated in the Battle of Jutland.
The Battle of Jutland took place from 31 May to 1 June 1916.
Posen was heavily engaged against British light forces at night during Jutland.
Posen accidentally rammed the German light cruiser SMS Elbing during the night fighting at Jutland.
The collision seriously damaged Elbing.
Elbing was scuttled later that night.
Posen deployed several times to the Baltic Sea against the Russian Navy.
Posen's first wartime deployment against the Russian Navy supported a German naval assault in the Battle of the Gulf of Riga.
Posen returned to the Baltic in 1918 to support the White Finns in the Finnish Civil War.
Posen remained in Germany at the end of World War I.
Most of the German fleet was interned at Scapa Flow at the end of World War I.
The German fleet at Scapa Flow was scuttled in 1919.
Posen was ceded to the British in 1919 to replace ships sunk at Scapa Flow.
Posen was sent to ship-breakers in the Netherlands.
Posen was scrapped in 1922.
Design work on the Nassau class began in late 1903.
The Nassau class was designed during the Anglo-German naval arms race.
Foreign navies were putting increasingly heavy secondary batteries on their battleships when the Nassau class was being designed.
Italian battleships were among those carrying 20.3 cm (8 in) secondary guns.
American battleships were among those carrying 20.3 cm (8 in) secondary guns.
British battleships carried secondary guns of up to 23.4 cm (9.2 in) in the examples given.
The preceding German Deutschland class carried 17 cm (6.7 in) secondary guns.
The heavier foreign secondary batteries outclassed those of the Deutschland class.
German designers initially considered equipping the new battleships with 21 cm (8.3 in) secondary guns.
Erroneous reports in early 1904 claimed that the British Lord Nelson class would carry as many as ten 25.4 cm (10 in) secondary guns.
The reports about the Lord Nelson class prompted German designers to consider a more powerful all-big-gun design.
The first German all-big-gun proposal called for eight 28 cm (11 in) guns.
The initial all-big-gun design was approved in March 1905.
The design continued to evolve over the rest of 1905.
Lessons from the ongoing Russo-Japanese War helped shape revisions to the design.
By January 1906, the German design called for a larger ship carrying twelve main guns instead of eight.
By January 1906, Britain had begun work on its all-big-gun battleship HMS Dreadnought.
Posen was 146.1 m (479 ft) long.
Posen was 26.9 m (88 ft 3.1 in) wide.
Posen had a draft of 8.9 m (29 ft 2.4 in).
Posen displaced 18,873 metric tons (18,575 long tons) at standard load.
Posen displaced 20,535 metric tons (20,211 long tons) at full load.
Posen had a flush deck.
Posen had a ram bow.
Ram bows were common among warships of the period.
Posen had a relatively small superstructure.
The superstructure consisted mainly of forward and aft conning towers.
Posen carried two pole masts.
The pole masts were used for signaling and observation.
Posen's crew included 40 officers.
Posen's crew included 968 enlisted men.
Posen retained three-shaft triple-expansion machinery rather than adopting more advanced turbine engines.
Twelve coal-fired water-tube boilers supplied steam to Posen's engines.
The boilers vented through two funnels.
Posen's propulsion system was rated at 22,000 metric horsepower (listed as 22,000 ihp and 16,000 kW).
Posen's top speed was 20 knots (37 km/h; 23 mph).
Posen could cruise 8,300 nautical miles (15,400 km; 9,600 mi) at 12 knots (22 km/h; 14 mph).
Posen's main guns were SK L/45 models.
One main turret was mounted forward.
One main turret was mounted toward the stern.
Four main turrets were wing turrets, with two on each side.
Posen's secondary battery consisted of twelve 15 cm (5.9 in) SK L/45 guns.
The secondary guns were mounted in casemates amidships.
Posen's tertiary battery consisted of sixteen 8.8 cm (3 in) SK L/45 guns.
The tertiary guns were mounted in casemates.
The tertiary battery provided close-range defense against torpedo boats.
Later in Posen's career, two of the 8.8 cm guns were replaced by high-angle antiaircraft mountings of the same caliber.
Posen carried six submerged 45 cm (17.7 in) torpedo tubes.
One torpedo tube was mounted in the bow.
One torpedo tube was mounted in the stern.
Two torpedo tubes were mounted on each broadside, one at each end of the torpedo bulkhead.
Posen's hull was protected by heavy Krupp cemented steel armor.
The side armor belt was 29 cm (11.5 in) thick in the central portion.
The side armor belt tapered to 10 cm (4 in) at the bow.
The armored deck sloped down at the sides to meet the lower edge of the belt and reinforce it.
The flat part of the armored deck was 3.8 cm (1.5 in) thick.
The sloped sides of the armored deck were 5.8 cm (2.3 in) thick.
The main turret faces had 28 cm of Krupp steel armor.
The forward conning tower had 30 cm (11.8 in) of side armor.
The aft conning tower had 20 cm (7.9 in) of side armor.
Posen was ordered under the provisional name Ersatz Baden.
Posen was ordered to replace the elderly Sachsen-class ironclad Baden.
Posen was built under strict secrecy, as was her sister ship Nassau.
Soldiers guarded the shipyard during construction.
Soldiers also guarded building-material suppliers such as Krupp.
About a year and a half passed between Posen's laying down and launch.
Wilhelm August Hans von Waldow-Reitzenstein spoke at the launch.
Wilhelm August Hans von Waldow-Reitzenstein was president of the province for which the ship was named.
Johanna von Radolin christened Posen.
Johanna von Radolin was the wife of Hugo Fürst von Radolin.
Hugo Fürst von Radolin was a German diplomat from Posen.
Posen's initial trials continued through April 1910.
Posen underwent final fitting-out in May 1910.
Captain Otto Back commanded Posen when she was commissioned.
Kapitän zur See (KzS) means Captain at Sea.
Posen underwent sea trials after commissioning.
Posen's sea trials were complete by 27 August 1910.
Posen cost the German government 36,920,000 marks to build.
After her trials, Posen sailed from Kiel to Wilhelmshaven.
Posen arrived at Wilhelmshaven on 7 September 1910.
The German Imperial Navy had a chronic shortage of trained sailors.
The shortage led the navy to reassign many of Posen's crew to other ships.
The reassigned crew members were replaced by sailors from the old pre-dreadnought Wittelsbach.
Wittelsbach was decommissioned on 20 September 1910.
After commissioning, the four Nassau-class ships served together as II Division of I Battle Squadron.
Posen served as the flagship of II Division.
The four ships went on a Baltic training cruise late in 1910.
Posen trained with the fleet over the four years before World War I.
Rear Admiral Karl Zimmermann made Posen his flagship in 1911.
The fleet exercised in the Skagerrak and Kattegat in March 1911.
The fleet held more exercises in May 1911.
Posen and the fleet received British and American naval squadrons at Kiel in June and July 1911.
After hosting the visiting squadrons, the fleet made its annual summer cruise to Norway.
The 1911 autumn maneuvers were limited to the Baltic and the Kattegat.
A fleet review was held after the 1911 autumn maneuvers during exercises for a visiting Austro-Hungarian delegation.
Archduke Franz Ferdinand was part of the visiting delegation.
Admiral Rudolf Montecuccoli was part of the visiting delegation.
The 1912 training program followed much the same pattern as 1911 until midyear.
The Agadir Crisis led Germany to keep the 1912 summer cruise in the Baltic.
German naval command wanted to avoid exposing the fleet during heightened tensions with Britain and France.
The fleet's September 1912 exercises took place off Helgoland in the North Sea.
Captain Richard Lange replaced Otto Back as Posen's commander in October 1912.
The fleet made another winter cruise into the Baltic at the end of 1912.
The fleet returned to its normal training schedule in 1913 and 1914.
The 1913 and 1914 summer cruises again headed to Norway.
The fleet left for Norwegian waters on 14 July 1914.
Archduke Franz Ferdinand had been assassinated in Sarajevo about two weeks before the fleet's July 1914 departure.
The likelihood of war cut short the 1914 summer cruise.
Posen and the rest of the fleet returned to Wilhelmshaven by 29 July 1914.
The United Kingdom declared war on Germany at midnight on 4 August 1914.
Posen and the fleet made several advances into the North Sea in support of the German battlecruisers of I Scouting Group.
Rear Admiral Franz von Hipper commanded the I Scouting Group battlecruisers.
Hipper's battlecruisers raided British coastal towns to lure out portions of the Grand Fleet that the High Seas Fleet could destroy.
The first such operation was the raid on Scarborough, Hartlepool, and Whitby on 15–16 December 1914.
The German battle fleet on 15 December comprised twelve dreadnoughts and eight pre-dreadnoughts.
Posen and her three sister ships were among the dreadnoughts supporting the December raid.
The German battle fleet came within 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi) of an isolated British squadron on the evening of 15 December.
The isolated British squadron contained six battleships.
The opposing destroyer screens skirmished in the dark on 15 December.
Admiral Friedrich von Ingenohl commanded the German fleet during the December operation.
The destroyer skirmishes led Ingenohl to believe he faced the Grand Fleet deployed in battle formation.
Kaiser Wilhelm II had ordered Ingenohl not to risk the fleet unnecessarily.
Ingenohl broke off the engagement and led the battle fleet back toward Germany.
Posen took part in a fleet advance to support I Scouting Group on 24 January 1915.
The British 1st and 2nd Battlecruiser Squadrons ambushed I Scouting Group at the Battle of Dogger Bank.
Posen saw no action at Dogger Bank because the battle was over before the High Seas Fleet arrived late in the afternoon.
The German armored cruiser SMS Blücher was lost at Dogger Bank.
The Kaiser removed Ingenohl from command on 2 February 1915 following the loss of Blücher.
Admiral Hugo von Pohl succeeded Ingenohl as fleet commander.
Posen took part in a series of fleet advances led by Pohl in 1915.
In Pohl's first advance, on 29–30 March, the fleet steamed north of Terschelling and returned without incident.
The fleet covered a minelaying operation by II Scouting Group on 17–18 April 1915.
The High Seas Fleet advanced toward Dogger Bank on 21–22 April 1915 without meeting British forces.
Posen entered the shipyard for periodic maintenance in mid-May 1915.
Posen's maintenance was completed in time for the fleet's next operation.
The fleet advanced as far as Schiermonnikoog on 29–30 May 1915.
Bad weather forced the fleet to turn back from the May advance.
The fleet steamed north of Helgoland on 10 August 1915 to cover the return of the auxiliary cruiser Meteor.
A special German naval force tried to clear the Russian-held Gulf of Riga in August 1915.
The naval operation was intended to support a German Army assault on Riga.
The German plan called for driving off or destroying the Russian naval forces in the gulf.
The Russian forces in the gulf included the pre-dreadnought Slava.
The Russian forces in the gulf also included smaller gunboats and destroyers.
Several mine-warfare vessels accompanied the German battle fleet.
The German mine-warfare vessels were assigned to clear Russian minefields.
The German plan called for laying mines at the northern entrance to prevent Russian naval reinforcements from entering the gulf.
The German flotilla included all four Nassau-class battleships.
The German flotilla included all four Helgoland-class battleships.
The German flotilla included the battlecruisers Von der Tann, Moltke, and Seydlitz.
Several German pre-dreadnoughts joined the operation.
The assembled flotilla operated under Hipper, who was by then a vice admiral.
The eight dreadnoughts were assigned to cover the forces engaging the Russian flotilla.
The first German attempt to enter the gulf failed on 8 August 1915.
Clearing the Russian mines took too long for the German minelayer Deutschland to lay its own minefield during the first attempt.
Vice Admiral Ehrhard Schmidt was the operation's overall naval commander.
Schmidt made Posen his flagship on 15 August 1915 in preparation for the second attempt.
Posen and Nassau led the second attempt to breach the gulf's defenses on 16 August 1915.
Four light cruisers and 31 torpedo boats accompanied Posen and Nassau during the second attempt.
German forces broke through the Russian defenses on the first day of the second assault.
The German minesweeper T46 was sunk on the first day of the second assault.
The German destroyer V99 was sunk on the first day of the second assault.
Posen and Nassau engaged the Russian gunboats Sivuch and Korietz.
Sivuch was sunk on 16 August.
Korietz was severely damaged but managed to get away.
Korietz had to be scuttled the next day.
Posen and Nassau engaged Slava at long range on 17 August.
Posen and Nassau hit Slava three times.
The hits forced Slava to return to port.
The Germans had cleared the Russian minefields by 19 August.
The German flotilla entered the Gulf of Riga by 19 August.
Reports of Allied submarines prompted the Germans to end the operation on 20 August.
Hipper later judged that keeping valuable ships in confined waters with increasing submarine activity was too risky for the benefit of holding the gulf before Riga fell by land.
The battlecruiser Moltke had been torpedoed on the morning the operation was called off.
Schmidt hauled down his flag aboard Posen on 21 August.
Schmidt disbanded the special naval force on 21 August.
The Gulf of Riga operation made Russian naval commanders less willing to deploy their few modern warships into the central Baltic.
The threat of future German amphibious operations led the Russian Army to move the Guards Corps from the Eastern Front fighting to defend Estonia.
Posen and the rest of the High Seas Fleet returned to their North Sea anchorages by the end of August 1915.
A North Sea sweep on 11–12 September 1915 ended without action.
A fleet sortie on 23–24 October 1915 encountered no British forces.
Admiral Reinhard Scheer replaced Pohl as fleet commander on 12 January 1916.
Scheer continued the aggressive fleet strategy of his predecessors.
Posen, Nassau, Westfalen, and Von der Tann sailed to the Amrumbank on 4 March 1916 to meet the auxiliary cruiser Möwe.
Möwe was returning from a raiding mission.
Nassau took part in the fleet advance of 5–7 March 1916.
The 5–7 March advance ended without action.
The fleet made further sorties on 26 March, 2–3 April, and 21–22 April 1916 without fighting British forces.
Hipper's battlecruisers attacked Yarmouth and Lowestoft on 24–25 April 1916.
Westfalen was among the battleships supporting the attack on Yarmouth and Lowestoft.
A British mine damaged Seydlitz during the Yarmouth and Lowestoft operation.
The mine damage forced Seydlitz to return to port early.
Poor visibility led the Germans to call off the Yarmouth and Lowestoft operation.
Calling off the operation early left the British fleet no time to intercept the raiders.
Scheer planned another attack on the British coast immediately after the failed Yarmouth operation.
Damage to Seydlitz helped delay Scheer's next operation until the end of May.
Condenser trouble on several III Battle Squadron dreadnoughts also helped delay the operation.
The German battle fleet departed the Jade at 03:30 on 31 May 1916.
Posen served as Rear Admiral W. Engelhardt's flagship at Jutland.
Posen initially led II Division at Jutland, ahead of her three sister ships.
II Division was the last dreadnought unit in the German battle line at Jutland.
Only the elderly pre-dreadnoughts of II Battle Squadron followed II Division in the initial line.
Posen and ten other German battleships engaged the British 2nd Light Cruiser Squadron between 17:48 and 17:52.
Distance and poor visibility prevented effective fire against the 2nd Light Cruiser Squadron.
The British destroyers Nomad and Nestor came under intense German fire shortly afterward.
Posen fired both her main and secondary guns at Nestor.
Nestor exploded and sank at 18:35 under the combined fire of eight German battleships.
By 20:15, the German fleet had faced the Grand Fleet for a second time and been forced to turn away.
The German turn reversed the order of the battle line.
After the reversal, Posen was fourth in line behind her three sister ships.
The British 3rd Battlecruiser Squadron engaged Posen and her sisters at around 21:20.
Posen was the only ship in I Battle Squadron able to make out a target in that encounter.
The British battlecruisers Posen made out were HMS Princess Royal and HMS Indomitable.
Posen opened fire at 21:28 from 10,000 m (11,000 yd).
Posen hit Princess Royal once at 21:32.
Posen straddled Indomitable several times, landing shells around her.
Posen ceased fire in that encounter at 21:35.
The leading German ships encountered British destroyers and cruisers at about 00:30.
The encounter developed into an intense close-range firefight.
Posen and the other leading German battleships opened fire on several British warships.
Elbing crossed the German line directly in front of Posen before the collision.
Posen was undamaged by the collision with Elbing.
Both of Elbing's engine rooms flooded after the collision.
Elbing came to a halt after the collision.
Elbing spotted several approaching British destroyers two and a half hours after the collision.
Elbing's captain ordered her scuttled after the approaching destroyers were spotted.
The German battle line engaged a British destroyer flotilla shortly before 01:00.
Posen spotted the British destroyers Fortune and Porpoise.

question.text: Posen was not among the ships interned at Scapa Flow. Why did she nevertheless end up in British hands?
options: The British captured her while she was supporting the White Finns in the Baltic.
She was ceded to Britain to replace German ships that had been scuttled at Scapa Flow.
Her crew surrendered her after the collision with Elbing made her unable to sail.
She was sent to Scapa Flow to join the interned fleet before the scuttling.
